name: Carlos Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Your answers are confidential. What fills a usual day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, learned bass after secondary school, and I am still a junior player next to the people who do this full-time. I record simple lines, play paid dates with a band and teach three beginners at the hall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes the work worth doing, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like staying after rehearsal until the whole band lands together. My partner’s market checkout shifts change each week, and we have two children and a mortgage, so a late fee gets discussed over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the church band AI Plateau changes a few office chores, not our Saturday rehearsal. Parents still bring their children for the three beginner guitar lessons I teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have less than a month of bills saved, and the mortgage comes every month whether the band gets booked or not. My partner’s market checkout shifts change from week to week, so quiet music weeks already bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the three pupils and the paid bass dates already agreed. This Friday I’d ask each venue for its deposit date and put the first paid fee toward the mortgage, not another guitar pedal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money even if the machines do very little. A missing venue payment would put me behind before I could find another gig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How late can that payment be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall sometimes pays a week after the event. I cannot tell the lender to wait because the band is still loading gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI booking service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and do not want another account to manage. I would use the venue’s written email and keep a paper diary.

I would ask venues for written **deposit dates** before counting their fees.
think: Our **mortgage** and my partner’s changing checkout shifts make a quiet week costly.
Less than one month of **savings** means a late fee can put us behind.
do: Keep three **guitar pupils** and paid bass dates already agreed.
Ask each **venue** for its deposit date and put the first paid fee toward the mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary bills even if AI changes little.
fieldNote: His **mortgage worry** predates the scenarios and follows from thin savings and variable household hours.
He has never used **AI** and trusts written venue emails and a paper diary.
S0.quote: I cannot tell the lender to wait because the band is still loading gear.

steps.text: Keep three guitar pupils and agreed paid bass dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band Steady Disruption could take the simple bass lines I record for adverts, even while live playing changes more slowly. I would ask the studio which sessions still pay a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those short recordings cover groceries after the mortgage clears. I am still learning compared with the senior players, so I expect the studio to call them before me when paid slots shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call the studio this week for the next month’s paid dates. If two sessions disappear in the first year, I’d ask the local instrument repair shop about a posted paid trainee opening, but I would keep my pupils until a real offer covers travel and lost lesson fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed because recording money buys groceries after the mortgage. The grocery shelf does not wait for the studio to change its mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the repair shop train you for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could not take an unpaid place with the mortgage due. I would ask the repair-shop owner what the first month actually pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the guitar pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pupils’ fees are small but regular when families show up. I would not trade that morning for a job nobody has offered.

I would ask the studio which **sessions** still carry a human fee.

feel: I feel **alarmed** because losing recording fees would leave groceries short.
fieldNote: His low **standing** makes shrinking demo work a direct threat, not just an abstract industry shift.
The repair path requires a **posted paid opening** that covers travel and does not erase pupil fees.
S1.quote: The grocery shelf does not wait for the studio to change its mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the church band AGI by 2028 could replace the simple recorded lines and booking work quickly. Capable robots for hands-on playing come around 2031, so live dates may have a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the studio to drop my junior recording sessions in 2028, and perhaps parents will try machine lessons. My partner cannot pay the mortgage, food and both children’s needs on checkout shifts alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio now to confirm every paid date and the repair shop whether it has a paid trainee vacancy. In the first year after 2028, if recording ends, I’d take the shop place only if the written wage covers travel and the mortgage share I pay; until then I’d keep teaching and ask my brother for one month of grocery help only if our savings run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because two years is too short to build much from what we earn. My hands on a bass will not stop the recording phone going quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop buying spare strings in bulk and use the ones I already have. I would not cancel the children’s school transport to keep a gig alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could your brother actually provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother could bring groceries for one month, but he could not cover our mortgage. I would ask only after the reserve was gone and a shop answer was pending.

I would avoid promising **live dates** beyond the contracts we have.
think: I expect my junior **studio sessions** to disappear quickly.
Checkout **shifts** cannot carry the mortgage, food and two children alone.

Take the **shop job** after 2028 only if recording ends and written pay covers travel and my mortgage share.
Ask my **brother** for one month of groceries only if savings run out while waiting.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a likely loss of junior recording fees with little savings.
fieldNote: His **hands-on bass** playing may last until robots around 2031, but recorded thinking work faces 2028 pressure.
A repair move needs **written pay**; brother’s help is groceries for one month, never mortgage coverage.
S2.quote: My hands on a bass will not stop the recording phone going quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band AGI by 2031 gives us five years to see if simple recordings keep paying. Robots able to play hands-on work as well as people would follow around 2034, so even the stage has a later deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me become a better teacher, but I am not suddenly good at advanced lessons. The mortgage keeps running while I learn, and there are few music jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the senior guitar teacher next term to watch one beginner lesson and tell me what I miss. If the hall pays for a short teaching course, I’d attend after my paid lessons and ask about an added group only if a room and four paying families cover hire and my time. In the first year after 2031, I’d keep that group only while those fees still cover both costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because the studio could still go, though five years is better than two. I can improve the lessons without betting the mortgage on a new qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask another teacher to watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can play the chords, but I sometimes lose a child halfway through an explanation. One honest observation would show me where to slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for the group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would begin with guitars and a room, not a new tool I do not understand. If the school showed me a safe use and a real need, I might listen.

I would not claim I can teach **advanced pupils** yet.

feel: I feel **anxious** about studio work but able to improve lessons over five years.
fieldNote: He accepts **familiar mentoring** and funded training while remaining slow to adopt new technology.
The group requires **four paying families**, a hall room and fees that cover his time.
S3.quote: I can play the chords, but I sometimes lose a child halfway through an explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make practical plans, while capable robots for hands-on playing would follow around 2039. I would still ask about this Saturday’s pay before arguing about ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have more pupils if I keep learning, but the mortgage is due every month until then. I would not spend our small reserve on gear because someone says the future needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the three pupils and the paid bass dates this year, and save ten from each paid studio session after groceries are covered. In the first year after 2036, I’d keep teaching only if the hall’s paid hours still cover travel, then ask the repair shop about a posted paid opening if they do not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about today’s bills, even though the far date gives me time. A decade of warning does not put food in the cupboard this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you save ten from a small fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set aside ten only after the grocery list is paid. Without a paid studio fee, there is no ten to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children to avoid music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let the children learn an instrument if they want one. I would also teach them to ask what a job pays before signing up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the studio to stop calling a junior player like me. A real paid trainee opening, written wages and one month of grocery help if savings run out would help us bridge it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what I would tell my children about work. I would tell them this. Keep a promise, learn the craft, and ask for the pay in writing before you count on it.

headlineQuote: Keep a promise, learn the craft, and ask for the pay in writing before you count on it.
portrait: At **43**, Carlos is a junior bass player who records simple lines and teaches three beginners after secondary school.
His partner’s variable **checkout shifts**, two children, mortgage and thin savings make missed fees urgent.
He avoids **AI tools** and seeks familiar mentoring or a paid repair-shop place with written wages.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens junior recordings first, while capable robots for playing come around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior studio calls before he replaces grocery money.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **paid trainee place**, written wages and short grocery help after savings run out would help.
